questions.q: What problem does MCP exist to solve?
options: The M x N integration problem: every AI application needing custom code for every service it connects to
The fact that LLMs cannot call any tools at all without MCP
A lack of JSON Schema support in programming languages
The need to train a separate model for every company
questions.explain: Without a shared standard, M applications each needing N services results in M x N bespoke integrations. MCP lets a service build one server that works with any MCP-compatible application.

questions.q: What is MCP's own official analogy for what it does?
options: A translator that converts one programming language into another
A USB-C port: a standardized way to connect, the same way USB-C standardized device connections
A firewall that blocks unauthorized tool calls
A database that stores every possible tool definition
questions.explain: MCP's documentation describes it explicitly as a USB-C port for AI applications: it doesn't add new capabilities, it standardizes how applications connect to the tools and data they need.

questions.q: Does a tool exposed through MCP use a different format than the tool schemas taught earlier in this course?
options: Yes, MCP tools cannot have a description field
No — an MCP tool still has a name, description, and JSON Schema input_schema, the same shape already taught
Yes, MCP replaces JSON Schema with XML
No, but MCP tools cannot take any parameters
questions.explain: MCP standardizes discovery and connection, not the tool definition shape itself. A tool's name/description/input_schema is the same format covered in the tool-calling chapter.

questions.q: Which of these is a real, documented example of what MCP enables, per its own published examples?
options: An agent accessing a user's Google Calendar and Notion to act as a more personalized assistant
A model that trains itself without any human-written code
Automatically translating any programming language into any other
Removing the need for tool descriptions entirely
questions.explain: MCP's own documentation lists this exact example, along with an AI coding tool generating a web app from a Figma design and enterprise chatbots connecting to multiple internal databases.

questions.q: Why does broad ecosystem adoption (Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor, and others all supporting MCP) matter practically?
options: It doesn't matter — adoption by one application is just as useful as adoption by many
It means a server built once works across every MCP-compatible application, not just the one it was originally built for
It means every application now has identical features
It means tool descriptions are no longer necessary
questions.explain: The actual payoff of a shared standard is the network effect: build an MCP server once, and it interoperates with every MCP-compatible host, not just a single hand-integrated application.
